subject: Geography
specVersion: Issue 4, February 2026 (first teaching September 2017, first examination June 2019)
statusNote: Rebuilt 9 Nov 2026 as the specification pupils sit, from the raw text (pdftotext) of the Pearson 4GE1 specification PDF, Issue 4: paper structure, marks, sections, all Topic 1 to 9 detailed content, fieldwork requirements (Sections B), AO weightings and the command word taxonomy (Appendix 3) were read. Points are paraphrased. Order follows the school's KS4 plan (Tarbiyyah Geography Curriculum Intent, written for AQA 8035, and Pearson's own 4GE1 Paper 1 and Paper 2 Section A schemes of work, which are generic) only where the content is on the 4GE1 specification: hazards first, then fragile environments and climate change, rivers, coasts and physical fieldwork in Year 10; urban environments, economic activity and energy and human fieldwork in Year 11. The earlier file taught AQA 8035 with a 4GE1 exam entry; AQA-only content (Paper 3 issue evaluation, glacial landscapes, cold environments) is no longer taught. Year and term placement is the school's sequence; Pearson allows any order.

sources.title: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE in Geography (4GE1) specification, Issue 4, February 2026
Pearson: information for centres entering private candidates

tiers: None (untiered, linear, graded 9 to 1; all papers at the end of the course)

assessment.title: Physical geography
assessment.content: Section A: two of river, coastal and hazardous environments (50 marks). Section B: one of three fieldwork questions on the same environments (20 marks).
assessment.format: Multiple-choice, short-answer, data-response and open-ended questions with a resource booklet; paper-based or onscreen. Available June and November.

assessment.title: Human geography
assessment.content: Section A: two of economic activity and energy, rural and urban environments (50). Section B: one of three fieldwork questions (20). Section C: one of fragile environments and climate change, globalisation and migration, development and human welfare (35).
assessment.format: Multiple-choice, short-answer, data-response and open-ended questions with a resource booklet; paper-based or onscreen. Available June and November.

nonExam: No coursework. Fieldwork is examined in Section B of each paper: one enquiry in a Paper 1 physical environment and one in a Paper 2 human environment, each with quantitative and qualitative primary data and at least two secondary sources. TGA pupils do both enquiries at home or locally, with a written guide and a live debrief.

aos.desc: Knowledge of locations, places, processes, environments and different scales
Understanding of concepts and the interrelationships between places, environments and processes
Interpret, analyse and evaluate geographical information and issues to make judgements (about 13% in fieldwork contexts)
Select, adapt and use skills and techniques to investigate questions and communicate findings (about 10% with fieldwork data)

units.title: Geographical skills (Appendix 4), taught throughout
points: Recognise and describe patterns of physical and human features on maps and atlases at different scales.
Draw, label and interpret sketch maps, diagrams, graphs and photographs, including satellite images.
Use grid references, scale, symbols and relief on maps, including digital maps and GIS.
Use simple statistics: means, medians, modes and lines of best fit.
Integrated skills in each topic: hydrographs, triangular graphs, population pyramids, footprint calculations.

units.title: Hazardous environments: some places are more hazardous than others
points: Characteristics, distribution and measurement of tropical cyclones, earthquakes and volcanoes.
Causes of tropical cyclones: ocean temperature, air pressure, wind shear and the Coriolis force.
Causes of volcanic and earthquake hazards: plate boundaries and hotspots.
units.option: Paper 1 Section A: two of Topics 1 to 3

units.title: Hazardous environments: impacts on people and the environment
points: Why people continue to live in areas at risk from hazards.
Why some countries are more physically, socially and economically vulnerable than others.
Shorter- and longer-term impacts of one earthquake, one volcano and one tropical cyclone.

units.title: Hazardous environments: managing earthquakes (case studies)
points: Preparation for earthquakes: warning, evacuation, building design, remote sensing and GIS.
Short-term responses and relief: emergency aid, shelter and supplies.
Longer-term planning: risk assessment, hazard mapping and rebuilding.
Case studies: earthquake management in a developed and in a developing or emerging country.

units.title: Fragile environments and climate change: environments under threat
points: Distribution and characteristics of the world's fragile environments.
Causes of desertification (drought, population, fuel, overgrazing) and of deforestation.
Natural causes of climate change and how human activity enhances the greenhouse effect.
units.option: Paper 2 Section C: one of Topics 7 to 9

units.title: Fragile environments and climate change: impacts
points: Social, economic and environmental impacts of desertification.
Impacts of deforestation: biodiversity loss, climate change, development and soil erosion.
Effects of climate change on fragile environments and people, including sea level and food supply.

units.title: Fragile environments and climate change: responses
points: How technology can resolve water shortages in areas threatened by desertification.
Approaches to sustainable use and management of a rainforest in a named region.
Responses to climate change by individuals, organisations and governments in two named countries.

units.title: River environments: the hydrological cycle
points: The hydrological cycle: characteristics, stores and transfers.
Drainage basin features: source, watershed, channel network and mouth.
Factors affecting river regimes, including storm hydrographs, land use, abstraction and dams.
units.option: Paper 1 Section A: two of Topics 1 to 3

units.title: River environments: processes and landforms
points: Fluvial erosion, weathering, mass movement, transport and deposition, and factors affecting them.
How channel shape, profiles, gradient, velocity, discharge and sediment change along a named river.
Upland and lowland landforms: valleys, interlocking spurs, waterfalls, meanders, oxbow lakes, flood plains, levees.

units.title: River environments: importance to people and management (case studies)
points: Uses of water, rising demand and supply; areas of water shortage and surplus.
Variations in water quality and the storage and supply of clean water.
Causes of river flooding and its prediction and prevention.
Case studies: river management in a developed and in a developing or emerging country.

units.title: Coastal environments: processes and landforms
points: Marine processes, weathering and mass movement at the coast, including longshore drift.
Influence of geology, vegetation, people and sea-level change on coasts.
Erosional and depositional landforms: headlands, bays, cliffs, caves, arches, stacks, beaches, spits, bars.
units.option: Paper 1 Section A: two of Topics 1 to 3

units.title: Coastal environments: coastal ecosystems
points: Distribution and features of coral reefs, mangroves, sand dunes and salt marshes.
Abiotic and biotic characteristics of one named coastal ecosystem.
Threats to coastal ecosystems from industry, farming, tourism and deforestation.

units.title: Coastal environments: conflicts and management (case studies)
points: Conflicts between coastal users over conservation or development.
Causes of coastal flooding and its prediction and prevention.
Soft and hard engineering and shoreline management plans.
Case studies: coastal management in a developed and in a developing or emerging country.

units.title: Paper 1 Section B: physical fieldwork enquiry
points: One enquiry with fieldwork in one Paper 1 environment (river, coast or hazards), answered in Section B.
Primary data must include quantitative and qualitative techniques.
Secondary data must use at least two different sources for the chosen environment.
Questions cover the pupil's own enquiry and unfamiliar data from the same environment.

units.title: Urban environments: urbanisation
points: Contrasting urbanisation trends over 50 years, including suburbanisation and counter-urbanisation.
Factors affecting the rate of urbanisation and the growth of megacities.
Problems of rapid urbanisation: congestion, transport, employment, crime and environment.
units.option: Paper 2 Section A: two of Topics 4 to 6

units.title: Urban environments: challenges (case studies)
points: Factors affecting urban land use: location, accessibility and land values.
Urban challenges in a named developed country: resource demands, waste and segregation.
Urban challenges in a named developing or emerging country: squatter settlements and informal economy.
Case studies: urban environments in a developed and in a developing or emerging country.

units.title: Urban environments: sustainable management
points: Development of the rural-urban fringe; greenfield versus brownfield sites.
Strategies to make urban living more sustainable and improve quality of life.
Roles of planners, politicians, developers and industrialists in managing urban challenges.

units.title: Economic activity and energy: economic sectors
points: Classification of employment into four sectors and differences by level of development (Clark Fisher).
Factors affecting the location of economic activity and how they change over time.
Reasons for changes in sector employment: raw materials, globalisation, mechanisation, policy.
units.option: Paper 2 Section A: two of Topics 4 to 6

units.title: Economic activity and energy: impacts of sector change
points: Impacts of sector shifts in a named developed and a named developing or emerging country.
Informal employment in a named megacity: causes and characteristics.
Malthus and Boserup on population and resources.

units.title: Economic activity and energy: energy (case studies)
points: Global variation in energy demand and production and the factors behind it.
Advantages and disadvantages of non-renewable and renewable energy sources.
Managing energy sustainably through education, efficiency and conservation.
Case studies: energy resource management in a developed and in a developing or emerging country.

units.title: Paper 2 Section B: human fieldwork enquiry
points: One enquiry with fieldwork in one Paper 2 environment (economic activity, rural or urban).
Primary data with quantitative and qualitative techniques; at least two secondary sources.
Questions cover the pupil's own enquiry and unfamiliar fieldwork data.

units.title: Rural environments (option not taught: school choice)
points: Biomes, ecosystem goods and services and farming systems.
Rural change in a named developed and a named developing or emerging country.
Diversification and sustainable rural strategies; roles of different groups.
units.option: Paper 2 Section A: not chosen (Topics 4 and 6 taught)

units.title: Globalisation and migration (option not taught: school choice)
points: Growth of the global economy; WTO, IMF and TNCs; push and pull factors of migration.
Impacts of globalisation, migration and tourism on different groups.
Managing trade, long-term migration and sustainable tourism.
units.option: Paper 2 Section C: not chosen (Topic 7 taught)

units.title: Development and human welfare (option not taught: school choice)
points: Defining and measuring development: GDP per capita, HDI, inequality and corruption indices.
Uneven development and its impact on welfare in one named country; demographic differences.
Aid, agreements and top-down versus bottom-up projects.
units.option: Paper 2 Section C: not chosen (Topic 7 taught)

commandWords.meaning: Recall or select one or more pieces of information
State the meaning of a term
Produce a numerical answer, showing working
Give similarities and differences, each point relating to both elements
Give an account of main characteristics or steps; no reasons needed
Give reasons why or how something happens, with justification
Apply understanding to give a reasoned explanation of what may happen
Break into parts and show how each contributes and how they interrelate
Use evidence to judge the relative significance of factors
Break an issue into parts and make evidence-based links between them
Weigh strengths, weaknesses and evidence to reach a substantiated judgement
Explore different sides of an issue through reasoning or argument

skills: Atlas, OS and digital map skills: grid references, scale, symbols, relief
Graphs and diagrams: hydrographs, triangular graphs, population pyramids, flow lines, proportional symbols
Photograph and satellite image interpretation, including GIS
Simple statistics: means, medians, modes, lines of best fit; carbon and ecological footprints
Fieldwork: enquiry design, data collection, presentation, analysis, conclusion and evaluation

prerequisites.from: Year 8 Spring 2: weather, climate and climate change (Geog.2 chapters 5 and 6)
Year 9 Spring 1: earning a living and globalisation (Geog.3 chapter 3)
Year 9 Autumn 2: natural resources and energy (Geog.3 chapter 2)
Years 7 and 8: map skills, GIS and home fieldwork

links.how: Geography explains urban growth and challenges; History supplies the 1854 cholera outbreak and John Snow's map

links.topic: Ecosystems, deforestation and the carbon cycle
links.how: Biology explains ecosystems and cycles; Geography explains threats to fragile environments and responses

links.topic: Energy resources and the greenhouse effect
links.how: Science explains energy transfers and greenhouse gases; Geography weighs energy mixes and security
Maths teaches averages and graphing; Geography applies them to fieldwork data

links.topic: Location of economic activity and globalisation
links.how: Business studies firms' location choices; Geography explains sector change and its impacts

contextNote: Climate change content (7.1) must be taught accurately, including natural causes and the enhanced greenhouse effect; teach what the specification requires. Hazard impacts are taught factually without distressing images.
gaps: Question papers, mark schemes and grade boundaries were not opened.

Option choices are the school's: Paper 1 rivers and coasts with hazards also taught (pupils answer two of three); Paper 2 Section A urban environments and economic activity and energy; Section C fragile environments and climate change. TO CONFIRM.
Case studies (four in-depth, a developed and a developing or emerging country in each paper) are not yet chosen: TO CONFIRM.
Fieldwork sites depend on where each pupil lives: TO CONFIRM a standard home or local enquiry pack for rivers or coasts and for an urban environmental quality survey.

Portal geography lessons (y10 52, y11 22) were written for AQA 8035: hazards, rivers, coasts, urban, resources and fieldwork lessons are reusable with 4GE1 command words; hot deserts, cold environments, Paper 3 and AQA-only case-study framing are retired or adapted (lessons are a later stage).
The school's KS4 Oxford AQA scheme (oxo_gegaq20 files) and the intent's AQA long-term plan are used for order and activities only where the content is on 4GE1.
